name: Li Béni Hesse

location.address: Rural path south of Bonnerue village, Houffalize, Province de Luxembourg

access: Free, on a public rural path leaving the village to the south; the trunk is ringed with barbed wire to protect it from damage, so viewing rather than touching.
transport: Rural path out of Bonnerue village, Houffalize; no public transport stop nearby, reachable on foot from the village.
story:
This beech has got smaller. It measured eight metres round at a metre and a half from the ground in 2007. In December 2023 it came in at 7.15 metres, because the southern side of the trunk had partially collapsed in the years between. The earlier readings show the climb up to that figure: 6.05 metres in 1977, 6.63 in 1996. It is still one of the largest beeches in Belgium, and it stood 17 metres tall when anyone last measured the height.

Li Béni Hesse is Walloon for roughly the blessed beech, and the blessing is the local half of the story. By tradition, funeral processions leaving Bonnerue for the cemetery at Vellereux stopped at this tree so the dead could be blessed on the way. The hollow trunk is said to hold a cross put there before the French Revolution, though nobody has documented it. The tree was pollarded during its working life.

Nobody has dated it. The damaged trunk also rules out working backwards from the girth, which is how a beech without papers usually gets an age. If you know when it went in, tell us.

The account of that 2023 visit describes one healthy section on the northern side, a dying branch to the west, and the tree standing and in leaf. Barbed wire is wound round the trunk to stop visitors damaging it further, so this is one to look at rather than touch.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, over seven metres round and broken away on its southern side, with barbed wire wound round it. It stands on the rural path leaving Bonnerue to the south.

name: Tilleul des Lognards

location.address: Grassy plateau between the village centre, Pierreux and the Bléron valley, Xhoris, Ferrières

access: Free, open rural plateau; the GR571 long-distance trail passes nearby and it is a signed local point of interest with the Sainte-Barbe chapel beside it.
transport: On foot from Xhoris village centre, on the GR571 trail; no public transport stop at the site.
story:
People came here to nail their illnesses into a tree. The Tilleul des Lognards was a nail tree: a cloth was rubbed on the sore place and then hammered to the bark, and the complaint was supposed to pass into the wood along with it. Skin trouble and toothache were the usual reasons for the walk up.

The lime stands on an open grassy plateau between the centre of Xhoris, Pierreux and the Bléron valley, and it has company. A Herman cross, the Sainte-Barbe chapel and a stele share the ground with it, so the tree is one item in a small collection of things people have put on this spot over the centuries.

Wallonia classified it on 5 November 1965 and it has been on the heritage register as an arbre remarquable ever since, under the reference 61019-CLT-0010-01. Its trunk measured four metres round at 1.30 metres from the ground in 2014.

Nobody has dated it. The French record allows that it may be very old and then declines to put a number on it, which is more honest than the number would have been. Every source calls it simply a tilleul, a lime, without saying which of the Tilia species it is. If you know either answer, tell us. The GR571 long-distance trail passes close by.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the company it keeps: a lime four metres round standing beside the Sainte-Barbe chapel, a Herman cross and a stele. It stands on the open plateau above Xhoris, near the GR571.

name: Tilleul de Macon

location.address: Place Yvon Paul, Macon, south side of the church, Momignies

access: Free, on the public village square beside the church.
transport: In the centre of Macon village, on foot; no public transport stop at the site.
story:
Twelve wooden posts hold this lime up: eight round the outside, four within, all of them standing on stone footings and last rebuilt in 1988. The tree is pruned every late autumn into three tiers of shrinking width, roughly eleven metres across at the bottom, about half that above it, and a terminal cluster at seven or eight metres up. It is a shaped tree, and it has been one for a very long time.

It went into the ground in 1714, and even that was a replacement. A lime stood on this spot in the fifteenth century and is named in the Besogne de Chimay of 1603. So the square at Macon has had a tree at its centre for at least six hundred years, and the one standing there now has held the post for about 310 of them.

Belgium classified it as a protected monument on 16 September 1942. Wallonia added it to its patrimoine exceptionnel in 2016, and in 2014 the ground beneath it was decompacted and its root zone protected, which is the unglamorous work that keeps a village tree standing.

Because it is pruned and propped rather than left to run, there is no single trunk measurement on record for it. It stands on the Place Yvon Paul, on the south side of the church, free to walk round at any hour.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its shape, three flat tiers of decreasing width propped on twelve wooden posts set on stone footings. It stands on the Place Yvon Paul, on the south side of the church.

name: Remarkable Lime of Chantemelle
access: Free, on the public village square.
transport: In the centre of Chantemelle village, on foot; no public transport stop at the site.
story:
Wallonia's classified heritage register knows this lime by a reference number, 85009-CLT-0008-01, and by the square it stands on. That is most of the file.

The square is the Place Saint-Michel, at the centre of Chantemelle in the commune of Étalle, in the province of Luxembourg. The tree also appears on the standing list of remarkable trees in Belgium, where it is given with its location and nothing else beside it, and it was photographed on the square in 2012.

What nobody has written down is the rest of it. No recorded age. No girth, no height. Every source calls it simply a tilleul, a lime, without naming which of the Tilia species it is, so even that is open.

A classification is not nothing, though. It means a public authority looked at this particular tree, on this particular square, and decided it was worth protecting. It stands on open ground at the heart of the village, free to walk up to at any hour.

So if you live in Chantemelle, or pass through it, the open questions are short ones: how far round is the trunk, how old do people there say it is, and what does the village actually call it. Tell us, and the entry gets better.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the square rather than by the tree: it is the lime on the Place Saint-Michel, standing on open ground at the centre of Chantemelle, and it carries Wallonia's heritage listing 85009-CLT-0008-01.

name: Arbre de la Liberté (Waremme)

location.address: Avenue Edmond Leburton 6, Waremme, on the paved plaza in front of the Maison Lejeune-d'Anglure

access: Free, on a paved public plaza/street frontage; the tree stands in front of the house, not inside its private grounds.
transport: In central Waremme, on foot from the town centre; no public transport stop at the site itself.
story:
This lime was planted to mark the anniversary of a republic that Belgium has not belonged to for two hundred years. On 22 September 1797, when Waremme and the rest of what is now Belgium were under French rule, it went into the ground as an arbre de la liberté, a liberty tree, on the anniversary of the founding of the French Republic. The regime it was planted for did not last. The tree did, and it is now about 230 years old.

It stands on the paved plaza in front of the Maison Lejeune-d'Anglure, a neoclassical house built around 1790, which makes the house the elder of the two by roughly seven years. The house has been classified heritage since 25 August 1987, though that protection is the building's and does not necessarily extend to the tree standing in front of it.

The position is worth knowing before you go. The tree is out on the street frontage rather than inside the private grounds, so you can walk right up to it from Avenue Edmond Leburton without asking anybody's permission.

Both sources call it simply a tilleul, a lime, and neither says which of the Tilia species it is. Nobody has taped its girth either. If you know, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: the lime out on the paved plaza in front of the Maison Lejeune-d'Anglure, the neoclassical house at Avenue Edmond Leburton 6, rather than inside its grounds.

name: Les Sept Frères de Gospinal

location.address: Opposite the Gospinal forestry house, between Jalhay and Solwaster, near the Hautes Fagnes

access: Free, beside a public nature-walking trail near the Hautes Fagnes.
transport: On a marked walking trail between Jalhay and Solwaster; no public transport stop at the site, reached on foot.
story:
A nineteenth-century lawyer who owned the Gospinal estate received his clients inside this oak. There was room. Cut back in the middle of the eighteenth century, it regrew as seven trunks that have since fused into one body 7.67 metres round, the largest multi-trunk oak in Belgium, and the reason it is called Les Sept Frères, the seven brothers.

It did other public work too. Officials of the communes of Sart and Jalhay used it as their meeting point when they argued out where the boundary between them ran.

The measurements are recent and they agree with each other. The ministerial order that made it a protected monument in 2012 records a girth of 7.44 metres; a visit in 2021 measured 7.67 at seventy centimetres from the ground, roughly a centimetre a year of new wood in between. It stands 26 metres tall. Wallonia had already classified it as a remarkable tree back in 1987.

The sign on site is blunt about the rest: over 300 years old, and nearing the end of its life. One of the seven trunks is dead and the others carry old wounds, though the account of that 2021 visit describes the canopy as still vibrant. Both of those things are true at once.

It stands opposite the Gospinal forestry house, on the walking trail between Jalhay and Solwaster near the Hautes Fagnes.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the seven trunks fused into a single body 7.67 metres round near the base, one of them dead. It stands opposite the Gospinal forestry house, on the trail between Jalhay and Solwaster.

name: Peace Oak of Wondelgem

location.address: Vroonstalledries, Wondelgem, between the Sint-Catharina parish church and the war memorial

transport: In Wondelgem, Gent; reachable on foot/by bike within the Vroonstalledries park, De Lijn bus stops nearby on Wondelgemkouter.
verify_notes: Planted in 1920 as a peace tree between the Sint-Catharina parish church and the natural-stone WWI war memorial on the Vroonstalledries, per the Flemish heritage inventory (inventaris.onroerenderfgoed.be, which specifically identifies the species as Quercus rubra, correcting the genus-only 'Amerikaanse eik' name). Vroonstalledries has been a protected cultural-historical landscape since 1953-08-13. Stad Gent's own 2026 news item confirms the park (and its monumental trees, this one included) is being actively renovated with a heritage management plan approved by the Flemish Heritage Agency in 2023, which is recent evidence the tree is standing and being cared for. Coordinates are the church's location as a proxy (Nominatim); marking approximate since I do not have the tree's own pin, only 'between the church and the memorial'.
write_pass_note: NOT WRITTEN: already published. This is the same tree as gnt_006 'The Peace Oak of Vroonstalledries' in data/cities/ghent.json, live with a story, a recognition line and a best_time. Same species (Quercus rubra), same planting year (1920), same position between the Sint-Catharina church and the war memorial on the Vroonstalledries, same heritage object (inventaris.onroerenderfgoed.be/erfgoedobjecten/300260), and 75 metres from the published pin, which is 'confirmed' there against 'approximate' here. name: Nagelboom van 's-Gravenvoeren

location.address: Heuvelke, at a crossing of two hollow roads, about 350m southwest of the Sint-Lambertuskerk, 's-Gravenvoeren, Voeren

access: Free, on a public path/hollow road crossing (thought to follow the Roman road Via Mansuerisca).
transport: On foot from 's-Gravenvoeren village, on a rural hollow-road crossing; no public transport stop at the site.
story:
At least eighty nails are hammered into the dead side of this horse chestnut, and that is the whole point of it. A nagelboom is a nail tree: you rub a nail over whatever hurts, then drive it into the trunk, and the ailment is supposed to travel into the wood along with it. The nails go into the back of the tree, where part of the trunk has already died, which is the part that takes them.

It stands where two hollow roads cross at the Heuvelke, about 350 metres southwest of the Sint-Lambertuskerk in 's-Gravenvoeren. The crossing is thought to follow the line of the Via Mansuerisca, a Roman road, which is a reading of the landscape rather than a settled fact.

Its condition is not good and both the Dutch record and the Flemish heritage inventory say so plainly. A successor has already been planted nearby against the day it goes. It was also a finalist for European Tree of the Year, which is a strange pair of things to be at the same time, and it is still standing.

Nobody has recorded its age or its girth. The nails are the only count anybody has taken of it, and they were put there one ailment at a time.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the nails, at least eighty of them driven into the dead back of the trunk. It stands where two hollow roads cross at the Heuvelke, about 350 metres southwest of the Sint-Lambertuskerk.

name: Dorpslinde van Massemen
access: Free, on the public village square.
transport: In the centre of Massemen village, on foot; De Lijn buses serve Massemen.
story:
In 2016 the country voted this lime its tree of the year, and the tree it beat into second place is called the Thousand-Year Oak of Lummen. The Summer Oak of Vollezele came third. The winner stands on the village square of Massemen and is 7.19 metres round under a crown only about 12 metres tall, which is a very wide tree on a short frame.

Its age came out of a laboratory rather than a guess. Ghent University dated it dendrochronologically in 2006 and put it between 378 and 440 years old, which places the planting in the second half of the sixteenth century or the very start of the seventeenth. The band is wide because that is what the method returns, and there is no tidier number to give. Either way it was a full-grown tree long before Belgium was a country.

A ministerial decree of 1 February 2001 protects the lime and the square together, as a monument and as a village landscape, so the setting around it is covered as well as the trunk. The measurements above were taken in 2007, so the girth has had nearly twenty years to move since.

It is on the Dorpsplein in the centre of the village, free to walk round, with De Lijn buses serving the village.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its proportions: a trunk 7.19 metres round under a crown only about 12 metres tall. It stands at the centre of the Dorpsplein in Massemen, on the open village square.

name: Solitaire Plane of Prudens Van Duyseplein
access: Free, centrepiece of a public square/roundabout.
transport: Central Gent, on foot or by bike; De Lijn tram/bus stops nearby.
story:
Five streets meet at the Prudens Van Duyseplein, and when the square was laid out in 1883 it was laid out around this plane. The tree is what would otherwise be a traffic island. It carries a clear stem of seven to eight metres before the first branch, then a crown that reaches 28 to 29 metres across at its widest, with a radius of eleven.

It is measurably still growing. The Flemish heritage inventory records it at 4.26 metres round in 2006 and 4.49 in 2013, both taken at a metre and a half from the ground, which is 23 centimetres of new wood in seven years.

Nobody has established when it was planted. A date of 1700 circulates, but it appears in none of the heritage records, so the honest answer is that this tree is undated. If you have seen a source that settles it, tell us.

What is documented is the protection, and it runs both ways. The plane has been a monument in its own right since 5 November 2013, and the square around it has been a protected townscape since April 1978. Locally it is not named after anybody. It is simply the tree of the square, which is what happens when a city builds a junction around a plane and then leaves it there for 140 years.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bare stem, seven to eight metres of it before the first branch, under a crown nearly 30 metres across. It stands alone in the middle of the Prudens Van Duyseplein, where five streets meet.
